topic: DP-3T: Tracking the Virus, Not the Person
target_audience: University students (Computer Science/Cybersecurity) and tech-savvy general public

outline.topic: DP-3T: Tracking the Virus, Not the Person
outline.target_audience: University students (Computer Science/Cybersecurity) and tech-savvy general public

sections.title: The Privacy Paradox: The Contact Tracing Challenge
sections.content: Introduce the conflict between public health (tracking virus spread) and individual privacy (avoiding a surveillance state). Define the goal: How can Bob know if he was near a COVID-positive Alice without a central server knowing where either of them was?
sections.example: Visual: Alice and Bob are represented as colored dots in a park. A 'Big Brother' eye tries to watch them, but a shield (DP-3T) blocks its view.

sections.title: Prerequisite: One-Way Hash Functions
sections.content: Explain the 'Digital Meat Grinder' concept. A hash function takes an input and turns it into a unique, fixed-length string. It's easy to go from 'Input -> Hash', but impossible to reverse 'Hash -> Input'. This is the foundation of identity protection.
sections.example: Graphic: A recipe (Secret Key) goes into a grinder (Hash Function) to produce unique sausages (Ephemeral IDs). You can't reconstruct the recipe just by looking at the sausages.

sections.title: Step 1: Local Key Generation (The Secret Seed)
sections.content: Every day, Alice’s phone generates a 'Secret Day Key' (SK). From this key, it derives multiple 'EphIDs' (Ephemeral IDs) that change every 15 minutes. These IDs are what the phone broadcasts via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE).
sections.example: Math Visual: SK_t = Hash(SK_{t-1}). EphID = Hash(SK_t || slot_number). Show a timeline where Alice's 'ID' changes from 'A1' to 'B7' to 'C9' throughout the day.

sections.title: Step 2: The Digital Handshake
sections.content: When Alice and Bob are near each other, their phones 'whisper' their current EphIDs to each other. Crucially, they only store the IDs they *receive* from others locally on their own devices. No location data or names are exchanged.
sections.example: Animation: Alice's phone sends 'X' to Bob. Bob's phone sends 'Y' to Alice. They both store these 'digital sticky notes' in a local 'Encounter Log' folder.

sections.title: Step 3: The Diagnosis and Decentralized Upload
sections.content: If Alice tests positive, she uploads her *Secret Day Keys* (for the period she was infectious) to a central server. Note: She does NOT upload her location or the IDs of people she met. The server only hosts a list of 'Infected Keys'.
sections.example: Visual: Alice sends a small 'Key' icon to a public cloud. The cloud now has a list of keys, but no idea who Alice is or who she saw.

sections.title: Step 4: The Local Match (Privacy Victory)
sections.content: Bob’s phone periodically downloads the new 'Infected Keys' from the server. Bob’s phone—and *only* Bob’s phone—recalculates the EphIDs that those keys would have produced and compares them to his local 'Encounter Log'. If there's a match, Bob gets an alert.
sections.example: Graphic: Bob's phone acts as a detective. It takes the public 'Infected Key', generates the corresponding EphIDs, and uses a magnifying glass to find 'X' in its own log. A match triggers a 'Low-Risk' or 'High-Risk' notification locally.

storyboard.title: The Privacy Paradox: The Contact Tracing Challenge
lecture_lines: Public health needs to track virus spread efficiently.
But surveillance states threaten our fundamental right to privacy.
DP-3T solves this by decentralizing all contact data.
Bob learns of exposure without anyone knowing his location.
animations: Show 'Health' #00FF00 and 'Privacy' #FF00FF icons on opposite sides with a white #FFFFFF dividing line. Highlight lecture line 1.
Display a large red #FF0000 eye above Alice #5555FF and Bob #FFA500 dots, shining light on them. Highlight lecture line 2.
Place a white #FFFFFF shield between the eye and dots; dots turn grey #808080. Highlight lecture line 3.
Alice and Bob dots move near each other then away; show distance arrow #FFFF00 but no coordinates. Highlight lecture line 4.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: One-Way Hash Functions
lecture_lines: Hash functions act like a digital meat grinder.
They turn unique inputs into fixed-length strings.
Going from input to hash is computationally simple.
Reversing a hash to find the input is impossible.
animations: Show 'Hash Function' box #FFD700 in center with 'Input' arrow. Highlight lecture line 1.
Move 'Secret Key' text #FFFFFF into box; '8f2b...' text #00FFFF exits. Highlight lecture line 2.
Show an 'Easy' checkmark #00FF00 next to the arrow pointing from Input to Hash. Highlight lecture line 3.
Show red #FF0000 'X' over a reverse arrow from Hash back to Input. Highlight lecture line 4.

storyboard.title: Step 1: Local Key Generation (The Secret Seed)
lecture_lines: Every day, Alice's phone generates a new Secret Key.
This key produces temporary IDs every fifteen minutes.
Alice broadcasts these rotating IDs via Bluetooth signals.
animations: Show phone screen with 'SK_t' key icon #FFD700. Highlight lecture line 1.
Animate 'SK_t' hashing into 'EphID_1' #00FFFF; show it changing periodically on a timeline #FFFFFF. Highlight lecture line 2.
Phone #808080 pulses blue #0000FF waves carrying the active 'EphID_n' #00FFFF. Highlight lecture line 3.

storyboard.title: Step 2: The Digital Handshake
lecture_lines: Nearby phones exchange their current anonymous IDs.
Devices only store the IDs they receive from others.
No names or location data are ever exchanged.
animations: Alice #5555FF and Bob #FFA500 phones exchange 'ID_A' and 'ID_B' icons. Highlight lecture line 1.
Bob's phone adds 'ID_A' #5555FF to a list labeled 'Encounter Log'. Highlight lecture line 2.
Red #FF0000 'Denied' effect over 'Name' and 'Location' text icons. Highlight lecture line 3.

storyboard.title: Step 3: The Diagnosis and Decentralized Upload
lecture_lines: After a positive test, Alice uploads her Secret Keys.
She only shares keys for her infectious period.
The server never learns who Alice actually met.
animations: Alice's phone #5555FF turns red #FF0000 and 'Share' button #00FF00 is pressed. Highlight lecture line 1.
Move 'SK_Alice' key icon #FFD700 from phone to Cloud icon #FFFFFF. Highlight lecture line 2.
Show 'Encounter Log' list #808080 staying on phone with crossed-out arrow to Cloud. Highlight lecture line 3.

storyboard.title: Step 4: The Local Match (Privacy Victory)
lecture_lines: Bob\u2019s phone periodically downloads the latest infected keys.
It reconstructs the IDs those keys would have generated.
It then compares these IDs against its local log.
If a match exists, Bob receives a private notification.
animations: Cloud #FFFFFF sends 'SK_Infected' #FFD700 to Bob's phone #FFA500. Highlight lecture line 1.
Inside Bob's phone, 'SK_Infected' hashes to produce 'Target_IDs' #00FFFF. Highlight lecture line 2.
Compare Bob's 'Encounter Log' #808080 to 'Target_IDs'. Highlight lecture line 3.
Matching entry #FF0000 flashes; phone displays a 'Notification' icon #FFFFFF. Highlight lecture line 4.
